promptText: What does temperature control in the sampling pipeline?
options: How many tokens the model is allowed to generate before stopping
How sharply peaked or flat the probability distribution becomes before a token is sampled, by dividing every logit by the temperature value before softmax
The maximum size of the model's vocabulary
Which specific words are banned from ever appearing in the output
explanation: Temperature divides every logit by T before softmax is applied; low T sharpens the distribution toward the single most confident token (approaching greedy decoding at T=0), while high T flattens it, making less likely tokens more competitive.

promptText: What does top-p (nucleus) sampling do differently from top-k sampling?
options: Top-p always keeps exactly the same number of candidate tokens regardless of context, while top-k varies the count

Top-p adaptively includes the smallest set of highest-probability tokens whose cumulative probability meets a threshold, so the candidate pool size varies per step depending on the model's confidence, unlike top-k's fixed count
Top-p and top-k are two different names for the exact same algorithm
Top-p only works with temperature set to exactly 0
explanation: Top-k always keeps a fixed count of candidates, which is too restrictive when the model is uncertain among many options and too permissive when it's highly confident; top-p adapts to the distribution's actual shape, narrowing when confident and widening when uncertain.

promptText: What happens when temperature is set to exactly 0?
options: The model refuses to generate any output at all
The model always selects the single highest-probability token deterministically (greedy decoding), since division by zero is special-cased rather than literally performed
The model samples uniformly at random from the entire vocabulary
The model's context window is automatically reduced to zero tokens
explanation: Dividing by zero is undefined, so implementations special-case T=0 as pure argmax selection (greedy decoding) rather than performing the literal division -- this is the limiting behavior the temperature formula approaches as T shrinks toward zero.

promptText: Why did the field move away from beam search for open-ended text generation like chat and story writing?
options: Beam search is too slow to run on modern GPUs

Beam search finds high-likelihood sequences, but human-written text is not itself the maximum-likelihood sequence of words, so beam search produces bland, repetitive, 'least surprising' text prone to looping
Beam search cannot be implemented for models with more than 10,000 vocabulary tokens
Beam search was replaced because it always produces factually incorrect answers
explanation: Beam search approximates the single most likely full sequence, but text that avoids all moderately-probable, 'surprising' word choices reads as robotic and prone to repetition -- stochastic sampling techniques (top-k, then top-p) were developed specifically to fix this degeneration.

promptText: What is the key difference between frequency penalty and presence penalty?
options: Frequency penalty only applies to punctuation, while presence penalty only applies to words

Frequency penalty scales with how many times a token has already appeared (compounding with each repeat), while presence penalty applies a flat, one-time penalty the moment a token appears at all, regardless of how many more times it recurs
They are two different names for the exact same mechanism
Presence penalty can only be applied to the first token of a response
explanation: Frequency penalty compounds with repeat count, making it effective against escalating repetition loops; presence penalty gives a flat one-time deduction regardless of subsequent count, making it better suited to encouraging lexical variety across the whole response.

promptText: Why is temperature 0 not a guarantee of bit-for-bit identical output across repeated hosted API calls?
options: Temperature 0 always produces completely random output, unrelated to determinism

Floating-point non-associativity, non-deterministic GPU kernel execution order, and provider-side batching/load-balancing can introduce tiny numerical differences that occasionally flip which token has the highest logit in a near-tie
Temperature 0 is not supported by any production API
APIs deliberately randomize output at temperature 0 to prevent caching abuse
explanation: Temperature 0 makes token selection deterministic given a fixed set of logits, but the logits themselves can vary slightly due to floating-point rounding order and batching differences on the serving infrastructure, occasionally flipping the argmax at near-tie steps.

promptText: In a multi-step agentic pipeline where one step parses user intent into a structured tool call and another step drafts a natural-language summary, why should these two steps use different sampling configurations?
options: Sampling configuration must always be identical across every step of a pipeline for consistency

The tool-call step should run at near-zero temperature and tight top-p because its output must parse as valid structured data with no upside to randomness, while the summarization step can use moderate temperature for natural lexical variety since no strict parser depends on its output
The summarization step should always run at temperature 0, while the tool-call step should use maximum randomness
Sampling parameters have no measurable effect on either step, so the choice is arbitrary
explanation: A single unexpected low-probability token in structured output (JSON, a function call) is far more likely to break a downstream parser than to add useful variety, whereas natural-sounding prose benefits from moderate temperature with no parsing risk -- applying one uniform profile across both either breaks the tool call or makes the summary stilted.

promptText: A distribution has probabilities [0.30, 0.25, 0.20, 0.10, 0.08, 0.05, 0.02] over its top seven tokens. What is the nucleus size at top-p = 0.5?
options: 1 token
2 tokens
4 tokens
7 tokens
explanation: Cumulative probability is 0.30 after token 1 and 0.55 after token 2, crossing the 0.5 threshold at token 2 -- so the nucleus contains exactly 2 tokens, illustrating how top-p's cutoff width emerges from the distribution's shape rather than being fixed.

promptText: Why can setting top_k=1 make it impossible to understand why carefully tuned temperature and top_p settings appear to have no effect?
options: top_k=1 disables temperature and top_p entirely at the API level, returning an explicit error
top_k=1 collapses the candidate pool to a single token before temperature or top_p have anything left to reshape or truncate, so sampling always picks that one token regardless of the other settings
top_k=1 only affects the first token generated, leaving all subsequent tokens unaffected
top_k=1 is not a valid configuration in any production API
explanation: Once top_k=1 has narrowed the candidate set to exactly one token, there is nothing left for temperature or top_p to reshape or truncate -- this is a common source of confusion when a stray top_k=1 from earlier experimentation silently overrides carefully tuned temperature and top_p values.

promptText: What is min-p sampling, and how does its selection rule differ from top-p?
options: Min-p keeps every token whose probability is at least min_p multiplied by the top token's probability (a relative floor that scales with confidence), whereas top-p accumulates cumulative probability mass to a fixed threshold
Min-p is identical to top-p but with the threshold direction reversed
Min-p always keeps exactly the same number of tokens as top-k
Min-p only applies when temperature is set above 1.0
explanation: Min-p sets a probability floor relative to the top candidate's probability (min_p x p_max), so the threshold automatically tightens when the model is confident and loosens when uncertain -- a different mechanism from top-p's fixed cumulative-mass sum, designed to behave more sensibly on flat, low-confidence distributions.

promptText: Why is nucleus (top-p) size at each generation step a useful production monitoring signal, independent of which token was actually sampled?
options: It has no diagnostic value; only the final chosen token matters for monitoring

Nucleus size is a direct proxy for model confidence at that step; a sudden shift in typical nucleus size for a fixed prompt template, with no prompt or model change, is an early signal that something upstream changed the model's actual confidence
Nucleus size only matters for billing purposes, not for quality monitoring
Nucleus size is always constant for a given top-p value, so tracking it provides no information
explanation: A nucleus of one or two tokens signals high model certainty, while a nucleus of dozens signals genuine uncertainty; tracking this cheaply computed signal over time can reveal a data distribution shift, prompt drift, or silent model version change before it shows up as a visible quality problem.

promptText: Why does the standard sampling pipeline apply temperature scaling before computing the top-p nucleus, rather than after?
options: The order makes no actual difference to the result in any case

Temperature scaling changes token probabilities nonlinearly via the exponential in softmax, which can change which tokens fall inside versus outside a cumulative-probability threshold; applying top-p first would compute the nucleus against the untouched distribution and then scale only within that already-fixed set, systematically narrowing the effective pool at high temperatures
Applying top-p before temperature would cause a division-by-zero error
The order matters only for top-k, never for top-p
explanation: Because temperature redistributes probability mass nonlinearly, a token just outside the p=0.9 nucleus at T=1 might fall inside it at T=1.5; scaling by temperature first ensures the truncation reflects the actual distribution shape intended for sampling, which is why every major inference stack applies temperature before top-p.

promptText: An evaluation dashboard shows a sudden, unexplained increase in output variance for a 'should be near-deterministic' endpoint, but deployment history shows no prompt, model, or sampling config change. What is the most rigorous investigative approach?
options: Immediately conclude the deployment history is complete and accurate, and assume the variance increase is a measurement artifact to be ignored

Re-verify directly against actual resolved request traces (not just the deploy log) that temperature, top-p, model version, and prompt are genuinely byte-identical to baseline, then consider provider-side causes outside the application's visibility -- a silent model update behind an unpinned alias, changed serving-side batching affecting floating-point non-associativity, or MoE routing behavior shifts from changed traffic composition
Immediately roll back the most recent code deployment regardless of whether it touched the affected endpoint
Assume the increase must be a random statistical fluctuation with no root cause, since deployment history rules out all possibilities
explanation: Deployment/config logs can miss changes made outside the normal pipeline, including provider-side silent model updates behind an alias, serving infrastructure changes affecting floating-point non-associativity, or Mixture-of-Experts routing shifts from changed concurrent traffic -- none of which would appear in the application's own deployment history since they originate entirely outside the system boundary.

promptText: How can Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routing introduce non-determinism at temperature 0 in a way that is mechanistically distinct from ordinary floating-point rounding?
options: MoE models do not support temperature 0 at all, so this scenario cannot occur

Batch-level factors (like expert capacity limits) can cause the same input token to be routed to a genuinely different expert sub-network depending on what else is in its serving batch, producing a materially different computation path -- not just a tiny numeric perturbation within the same computation graph, but a different graph entirely
MoE routing only affects output length, never which token is selected
MoE routing is always identical regardless of batch composition, making this a non-issue
explanation: Floating-point non-associativity perturbs numbers within the same computation graph, while MoE batch-dependent routing (driven by expert capacity limits under different concurrent traffic) can select an entirely different computation graph for the same token, producing different logits and potentially a different argmax result even at temperature 0 -- a distinct architectural mechanism, not a numerical precision issue.

promptText: A teammate argues 'we should just always use temperature 0 everywhere for consistency and safety.' What is the strongest, most complete rebuttal?
options: Temperature 0 is always the correct choice for every task, so no rebuttal is needed

Temperature 0 is right for tasks with one correct answer, but actively harmful for tasks needing variety or exploration (brainstorming, diverse candidate generation), and it can amplify failure modes -- a model stuck in a bad pattern at temperature 0 will deterministically repeat that exact mistake on retry, whereas nonzero temperature gives a regeneration attempt a genuine chance to escape it
Temperature 0 should never be used anywhere because it always produces worse output than higher temperatures
Temperature has no relationship to safety or determinism, so the argument is entirely irrelevant
explanation: Sampling configuration should be chosen per task against measured criteria, not applied as a single global rule; temperature 0 is appropriate for structured extraction, classification, and tool calls, but harmful for exploratory tasks, and it can also trap a retry in the exact same deterministic mistake rather than allowing escape via controlled randomness.
